briefing.text: The expected value in observed/expected must be distance-matched. Confirm from the data that the pixel (bin 8, bin 17) at 20 kb sits on the diagonal dist_bin = 9, and that the dist_bin column equals bin_j - bin_i. The expected for that pixel is then computed from pixels on that same diagonal only, within the same replicate, after the same normalization as the observed value (the cooltools expected_cis convention). Do not use a whole-matrix mean, pool several diagonals into one average, or borrow an expected from another replicate or another resolution.
briefing.reason: The choice of expected defines the reported quantity; a global or mis-matched expected turns log2(O/E) into a measure of distance decay rather than loop enrichment.

briefing.text: Compute everything per replicate first, then average. The four replicates (two control, two case) can differ in sequencing depth and in the shape of the distance-decay curve P(s), so comparing raw counts or pooled matrices confounds depth or P(s) differences with loop differences. Check total counts and log-log P(s) slopes for each replicate. Compute the expected within each replicate (O/E then normalizes itself for depth), take log2(O/E) per replicate, and take the arithmetic mean of the two log2 values per condition; delta is the case mean minus the control mean. The mean of log2(O/E) is not the same as log2 of the mean O/E or log2 of O/E on summed replicates, so do not sum replicates first. Look at the target pixel's count in every replicate and at zeros on its diagonal: a zero gives -inf, so use a pseudocount only if a zero actually occurs, and state it. Report the spread between replicates within each condition; a joint normalization across replicates (multiHiCcompare-style loess) can serve as a sensitivity check.
briefing.reason: The order of operations (log then average, per replicate) changes the numbers, and the task defines the quantities as means of per-replicate log2(O/E); depth or P(s) differences between conditions would otherwise leak into delta.

briefing.text: Raw Hi-C counts carry per-bin visibility biases. The 20 kb bin annotation file gives gc_content, mappability and re_sites (restriction-site density) for each bin, so O/E computed on raw counts may reflect bias at the two anchor bins rather than looping. Per replicate, correlate bin coverage (row sums) with gc_content, mappability and re_sites, and compare the row sums of bins 8 and 17 with the other bins. If bias is present, correct for it before computing O/E: either balance each replicate's matrix (ICE/Sinkhorn, cis-only, excluding the shortest 1-2 diagonals) or fit an explicit Poisson/negative-binomial model with log(gc), log(mappability) and log(re_sites) as covariates. Compute observed and expected on the same corrected scale, and report both the raw and the corrected values.
briefing.reason: Whether the reported loop strength is computed on raw or bias-corrected counts can change all three numbers; the bin covariates are supplied in the data and should not be ignored without a check.

briefing.text: Low-quality bins and short-range diagonals distort both balancing and the expected. Flag bins with low mappability or with log-coverage far below the median (about 5 MAD or more), mask them (set to NaN) and leave them out of the per-diagonal expected averages. Check specifically whether bin 8 or bin 17 is itself flagged. The shortest diagonals (distance 0-1 bins) carry self-ligation and undigested-fragment artefacts and should be ignored when balancing (the cooltools default is ignore_diags=2); note that the contact table has no main diagonal (dist_bin starts at 1), so adapt the balancing accordingly.
briefing.reason: Bad bins left in the matrix shift the balancing weights and the diagonal-9 expected, and a flagged anchor bin would change how far the result can be trusted.

briefing.text: The 20 kb matrix has only 24 bins, so the diagonal at distance 9 has only about 15 pixels (fewer after masking). The expected there is noisy, is pulled up by the target pixel itself if that pixel is enriched, and can be skewed by other loops, domain structure, edge bins or bad bins. Count the valid pixels on diagonal 9 in each replicate and compare the diagonal mean with the median, with and without the (8,17) pixel; also compare with a smoothed P(s) (log-log regression or loess across diagonals; cooltools smooths P(s) by default). These are still distance-matched expecteds, so they do not conflict with the rule against pooling diagonals into a single mean. Choose and justify one definition of the expected as primary before comparing conditions, state which one was used, and report how much the three quantities move under the alternatives.
briefing.reason: With about 15 pixels per diagonal, the choice between plain mean, median, target-excluded mean and smoothed expected can visibly move the answer, so the choice must be deliberate and its sensitivity reported.

briefing.text: A diagonal (global) expected marks every pixel inside a contact domain as enriched, so a high O/E is not by itself evidence of a focal loop. Loop callers (HiCCUPS, cooltools dots) compare the pixel with a local background instead. As QC, compute the enrichment of the (8,17) pixel against a donut neighbourhood (for example a ring of pixels 1-3 bins away, excluding the peak's own row and column) and compare it with the diagonal-expected O/E in each replicate. If the two diverge, keep the diagonal-expected O/E as the primary result, because the task asks for observed/expected, and report the local enrichment as QC. State whether any case-control difference looks like a focal loop change or a broad domain-level change.
briefing.reason: It determines how the reported numbers should be interpreted and guards against describing a domain-wide change as a loop change.

briefing.text: Measured loop signal depends on resolution, and a loop anchor that is split across two 20 kb bins or sits one bin off shifts the enrichment at the named pixel. Inspect the 3x3 neighbourhood around (8,17) at 20 kb in each replicate to see whether the peak is centred on that pixel. Cross-check with the 40 kb data: find the 40 kb pixel that contains the two 20 kb bins by matching genomic coordinates in the two bin annotation files (the library suggests 40 kb bins 4 and 8, but this is unverified, so confirm by coordinates rather than by index arithmetic), and check that the case-control direction agrees. Expect a smaller fold change at 40 kb. Still report the 20 kb (8,17) pixel as the task asks; record any peak offset or disagreement between resolutions in the QC.
briefing.reason: The task supplies 40 kb data that is otherwise unused; it is the available independent check on the 20 kb estimate, and an off-centre peak would change how the result is qualified.

questions.question: QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team found that the two anchor bins (8 and 17) have unusually high gc_content compared with the other bins, and that contact counts depend on GC in every replicate. Check whether that holds in your data, and whether any dependence of your balanced values on the GC of the two bins remains after ICE (for example among the diagonal-9 pixels you average for the expected). Does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team observed that ICE balancing on this truncated 24-bin window can be distorted by edge bins (which see only part of their contacts) and by the loop pixel's own contribution to the coverage of bins 8 and 17. Check in your data how the balancing weights of bins 8 and 17 and of the edge bins compare with the rest, and whether those weights change if the target pixel is left out of the balancing. Does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team left the target pixel (8,17) out of the data used to build the expected, whereas your primary expected is the diagonal-9 mean with that pixel included among only 11 valid pixels. You recorded that your result moves when the target is left out. Check how much of the diagonal-9 mean in each replicate comes from the target pixel itself, and state which definition of 'expected' you judge the task to mean and why. Does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team found that only 11 valid pixels remain on diagonal 9 once bins 10 and 11 are masked, that the result moves with how the diagonal-9 expected is defined (mean, median, target left out, smoothed across distances), that the distance-decay slope differs between case and control, and that control replicates have zero pixels at long range. Check whether these hold in your data, how many pixels actually determine the distance-9 factor in your GLM, and whether the long-range zeros or the differing decay affect the fit. Does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team corrected per-bin bias by balancing each replicate rather than with a single covariate, and found that bin coverage is strongly related to mappability, driven by bins 10 and 11. Your GC effect is one linear coefficient shared across all distances and fit on about 250 pixels. Check whether that coefficient is stable when it is estimated without the influence of particular bins (for example the edge bins or bins neighbouring 10 and 11), whether it is separable from mappability and re_sites in these 24 bins, and whether residual per-bin bias remains at bins 8 and 17 after your model. Does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team used two cross-checks you did not record: a local (donut) background around pixel (8,17) to tell a focal loop from broader domain enrichment, and the 40 kb pixel covering the same coordinates as a consistency check on the 20 kb estimate. Check whether your expected and your per-condition values are consistent with those two views in your data. Also state whether you judge that the task's 'expected' should include or exclude the target pixel, and why. Does it change your method?

referee.difference: Both teams mask bins 10/11, use per-replicate expected from the other 10 valid diagonal-9 pixels (target left out), and average log2 O/E per condition. The only difference is the bias model: X uses per-bin ICE visibility factors (target pixel excluded from balancing), giving 1.93/-0.29/2.22; Y uses an NB GLM with distance factors plus one summed-anchor-GC covariate, giving 1.84/-0.15/1.98.
referee.test: test.py: in each replicate, fit an NB GLM (alpha 0.05) on dist>=2 pixels without masked bins and without the target. Model A has diagonal factors plus GC-sum (Y). Model B has diagonal factors plus per-bin factors (X/ICE-equivalent). Held out each non-target pixel in anchor rows 8 and 17 (dist 2-15, 136 pixels over 4 reps) one at a time, predicted it, and compared NB deviance with a paired sign-flip permutation test. Also compared AIC and the target O/E under each model.
referee.expected_if_x: If anchor bins 8/17 carry visibility bias that GC does not explain, the per-bin model predicts held-out anchor-row pixels clearly better (lower deviance, significant), and that supports X.
referee.expected_if_y: If GC accounts for the anchor bias, the GC model predicts as well or better with fewer parameters, and that supports Y.
referee.outcome: Mean held-out deviance was 1.58 for GC and 1.72 for per-bin. The paired difference -0.135 had p=0.17, so it was not significant. Per-bin was better on 44% of pixels. GC was better in the controls; the two were equal in case. AIC favoured GC in ctrl_r1 and ctrl_r2, per-bin in case_r1, and tied in case_r2. The target log2 O/E reproduced both teams: GC model 0.18/-0.48/1.74/1.88; per-bin model -0.01/-0.45/1.88/2.00.
referee.reason: The disagreement comes entirely from choosing between two defensible bias corrections. The held-out test slightly favours GC-only in the controls, but not significantly, and the case replicates do not separate the models. The data cannot settle which bias correction is right, so neither answer is shown to be better. Both agree on a focal case-specific loop: delta about 2.0-2.2, case about 1.8-1.9, control about -0.15 to -0.3.
